title: Letting Astra loose inside an already in-development game
author: AlgaeNo3373
selftext:
*No one-shot cheetahs, sorry, whales are much easier to animate, and I wanted one ;p*

So far the game's been made by Claude Code so Astra just got hotdropped into things with a welcome note from Claude and a letter from another GPT instance insisting that their first task was some kind of machine-god-given rite. The game takes place inside a representation of GPT-2 Small's internals ysee, where neurons are being represented as *stars*, so it's kind of absurdly on-theme for Astra (latin for star, in case you didn't know) to have the honors here, and turn our placeholder red dots into something astral. New in-game lore is thusly:  


>On the first day they lit stars. And then, Astra rested, for the user was out of credits.

The whole pass was about half my weekly usage FYI. Have only done about 8 turns of visual passes at this point but it's already been a big improvement. 

A few notes on different features getting into some details:

* Adding glow to stars/lines might seem trivial but the ask was more complicated. I wanted it to look good and cost basically nothing, so a big focus on performance. We need to support as much as 36,000 in scene at a time, and be able to physically re-arrange and move hundreds of them about at a time, quickly and fluidly, all while hitting the player's GPU with tensor math for LLM analysis (can be costly). Astra did a lot of clever stress testing on the way to getting this working, and in doing so, found other VFX optimization in my code base (overly-aggressive/distant rendering of neuron ID labels caused unnecessary slowdown). 
* Next up was adding a "vector field" with FOV changes, slowdowns, small elements we try to stack on top of each other (Claude's suggestion, based on best practices in gamedev when designing things like movement). It's helpful giving the place some life and makes movement a little juicier, at least. I also wanted to marry the neuron "hit count" - how many times a given phrase activated a specific neuron - with the field's flow, so "busy" neurons get a lot of vectors, which is visually showing what's literally happening. Astra kinda nailed all this, which is v promising for using more VFX in targeted ways like this in future runs.  
* Next test was 3D assets. I want a giant whale as a background set piece, and a bar where NPCs can come and go. Claude did an online search on what folks were doing, rated Astra's ability to do this more simply, and suggested among two paths, the idea of skipping Blender entirely for a first attempt using procedural GDscript - a "terraced/voxel whale body directly in code via Godot". We've avoided expensive assets so far, may as well keep trying. 
* I pulled two images from the same Midjourney SREF, one of whale, one of a bar. Each model was iterated on once by Astra before I locked it in as first draft. I was impressed with both, as someone who can't model. Each is something I'd happily pay for. I'm happy with the animation too. 
   * I've tried this exact thing before with Claude Code btw, and what usually happens is I get a) a malformed animal and b) it's not true 3D, just a very thick 2D "flat" object. What Astra did here was very different. The whale is not symmetrical (not obviously just a copy of half an axis, doubled). It's shaped like it should be, with variation all over. 
   * For the whale, a single indexed mesh with 18,028 triangles plus one MultiMesh of 96 five-triangle fish
* The bar was similarly impressive to me. \~10,000 triangles, a detailed little set piece inside the same art direction, with its own lighting touches. 
* Everything added in-game came with sliders/controls for things, so I could position it, change brightness, etc. I recommend same if you're not familiar with your engine/editor. I'm new to Godot so in-game method is perfect, if a little extra framework to setup. 



Astra feels like the start of a paradigm shift, to me. The spatial awareness is really impressive and has many implications we'll need time to appreciate and get the best out of, I reckon. I'm struck also by how it already has completed some games (portal for example). In game-playing terms there is an agent made by DeepMind called "SIMA" (Scalable Instructable Multiworld Agent). It's something I check in on now and then because when agents can play games well enough, that has big implications for gamedev. I did not expect to be able to access a SIMA-like agent this soon, on a $30 plan. Astra's ability to playtest my game while it builds inside it is quite powerful, imvho. 



Anyways just adding my Astra first impressions to the pile here, happy tinkering :)
